s0003.literal: Dao Zhongju; Han Zigao; Hua Jiao
s0003.idiomatic: Dao Zhongju; Han Zigao; Hua Jiao

s0004.literal: Dao Zhongju, styled Deyan, was a native of Wuyuan in Pengcheng.
s0004.idiomatic: Dao Zhongju, styled Deyan, came from Wuyuan in Pengcheng.

s0005.literal: His grandfather Tan was Secretariat Attendant of Qi.
s0005.idiomatic: His grandfather Tan had been Qi’s secretariat attendant.

s0006.literal: His father Qia was Palace Attendant of Liang.
s0006.idiomatic: His father Qia was a palace attendant under Liang.

s0007.literal: Zhongju had no other art or profession, yet in establishing himself he was upright and steadfast.
s0007.idiomatic: Zhongju had no special craft, but he stood upright in his conduct.

s0008.literal: He doffed the commoner's garb as Editorial Officer of Writings, Palace Gentleman in Attendance, and Chief Clerk of the Prince's establishment.
s0008.idiomatic: He entered service as editorial officer of writings, palace gentleman in attendance, and chief clerk of a princely establishment.

s0009.literal: He went out as magistrate of Changcheng; his governance was famed for integrity and fairness.
s0009.idiomatic: Posted as magistrate of Changcheng, he won a name for honest, even rule.

s0010.literal: When Emperor Wen was in the countryside, he once visited Zhongju. The sky was cloudy and rainy; Zhongju sat alone in his study and heard outside the walls the sound of flutes and drums. Presently Emperor Wen arrived. Zhongju thought it strange and thereafter bound himself to him in deep trust.
s0010.idiomatic: While Emperor Wen was still in the countryside he once called on Zhongju. Rain fell under a leaden sky. Zhongju sat alone in his study and heard flutes and drums beyond the wall. Then Emperor Wen arrived. Struck by the omen, Zhongju gave him his deepest trust.

s0011.literal: Emperor Wen once lodged in Zhongju's tent after drinking by night. Suddenly a divine light of five colors shone within the room; from this his reverent service grew still more deferential.
s0011.idiomatic: Emperor Wen once spent the night in Zhongju’s tent after wine. A five-colored light suddenly filled the room. From then on Zhongju served him with still greater reverence.

s0012.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion Zhongju attached himself to Emperor Wen.
s0012.idiomatic: When Hou Jing rebelled, Zhongju cast his lot with Emperor Wen.

s0013.literal: When Jing was pacified, Emperor Wen became administrator of Wu Commandery and made Zhongju deputy administrator; together with Yu Chi of Yingchuan he were both Emperor Wen's clients.
s0013.idiomatic: After Jing fell, Emperor Wen became administrator of Wu Commandery and made Zhongju his deputy. He and Yu Chi of Yingchuan both served as Emperor Wen’s clients.

s0014.literal: When Emperor Wen was General Who Displays Martial Resolution, he made Zhongju chief clerk; soon he also held concurrently the magistracy of Shanyin.
s0014.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen was made general who displays martial resolution, he named Zhongju chief clerk and soon gave him the magistracy of Shanyin as well.

s0015.literal: When Emperor Wen succeeded to the throne, [Zhongju] was appointed Palace Attendant and took part in managing selection affairs.
s0015.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen took the throne, Zhongju was made palace attendant and helped manage appointments.

s0016.literal: In the first year of Tiancheng, he was made acting Minister of the Masters of Writing for Officials, enfeoffed Marquis of Bao'an county with a fief of five hundred households.
s0016.idiomatic: In Tiancheng year 1 (560) he was made acting minister of the masters of writing for officials and enfeoffed as Marquis of Bao’an with five hundred households.

s0017.literal: In the third year he was appointed Minister of the Masters of Writing for Officials.
s0017.idiomatic: In the third year he was appointed minister of the masters of writing for officials.

s0018.literal: That year he was transferred to Vice Director of the Masters of Writing (right) and Metropolitan Governor of Danyang; his participation in government remained as before.
s0018.idiomatic: That year he was made right vice director of the masters of writing and metropolitan governor of Danyang, with the same role in government as before.

s0019.literal: Soon his enfeoffment was changed to Marquis of Jianchang county.
s0019.idiomatic: Soon his title was changed to Marquis of Jianchang.

s0020.literal: Zhongju had no learning or scholarship; court regulations were not his strength—all selections and appointments issued from Yuan Shu.
s0020.idiomatic: Zhongju had no learning and court law was not his field. Every appointment came from Yuan Shu.

s0021.literal: By nature he was spare and simple, did not meddle in worldly affairs, and was intimate with no court officials; he merely amassed wealth and drank deep—that was all.
s0021.idiomatic: He was spare by nature, kept out of public business, and was close to no courtier. He only hoarded money and drank.

s0022.literal: In the sixth year his term expired and he was relieved of the metropolitan governorship.
s0022.idiomatic: In the sixth year his term ended and he left the metropolitan governorship.

s0023.literal: At that time Emperor Wen had been bedridden with illness for years and did not personally oversee the myriad affairs of state; matters within the Masters of Writing were all left to Zhongju to decide.
s0023.idiomatic: By then Emperor Wen had lain ill for years and no longer ran the realm himself. Everything in the masters of writing went to Zhongju for decision.

s0024.literal: In the first year of Tiankang, he was transferred to Palace Attendant and Vice Director of the Masters of Writing; his participation in government remained as before.
s0024.idiomatic: In Tiankang year 1 (566) he was made palace attendant and vice director of the masters of writing, with the same powers as before.

s0025.literal: When Emperor Wen's illness grew grave, [Zhongju] entered to attend him with medicine.
s0025.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen grew desperately ill, Zhongju entered to nurse him with medicine.

s0026.literal: When Emperor Wen died, Emperor Xuan received the testamentary edict as Director of the Masters of Writing and entered to assist in government. Zhongju, together with Left Assistant Wang Xian, Secretariat Attendants Liu Shizhi and Yin Bujiu, and others—because public expectation had a direction—then sent Bujiu to counterfeit an imperial order and send Emperor Xuan back to the Eastern Mansion.
s0026.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen died, Emperor Xuan took the testament as director of the masters of writing and entered to govern. Zhongju, with the left assistant Wang Xian and secretariat attendants Liu Shizhi and Yin Bujiu, judged where the court’s hopes lay and sent Bujiu to forge an edict ordering Emperor Xuan back to the Eastern Mansion.

s0027.literal: When the affair was exposed, Shizhi was sent to the northern prison and granted death; Xian and Bujiu were both handed over for prosecution. Then Zhongju was made General of Steadfast Resolution and Grandee with the Gold Seal and Purple Ribbon.
s0027.idiomatic: When the plot came out, Shizhi was sent to the northern prison and granted death. Xian and Bujiu were handed over for trial. Zhongju was reduced to steadfast-resolution general and grandee with the gold seal and purple ribbon.

s0028.literal: Earlier, Zhongju's son Yu had married Emperor Wen's younger sister, Princess Xin'an the Long of Xinyi; he reached the post of Attendant Gentleman of the Secretariat, went out as Administrator of Xuancheng; Emperor Wen supplied him with warriors and horses. That year he was transferred to Interior Minister of Nankang; because of the state mourning he had not yet taken up the appointment.
s0028.idiomatic: Earlier Zhongju’s son Yu had married Emperor Wen’s sister, Princess Xin’an the Long of Xinyi. He rose to attendant gentleman of the secretariat, then went out as administrator of Xuancheng, and Emperor Wen gave him troops and horses. That year he was named interior minister of Nankang but had not yet taken office because of the state mourning.

s0029.literal: Zhongju, having been set aside and living in a private residence, and Yu both felt ill at ease.
s0029.idiomatic: Zhongju, dismissed and living at home, and Yu both felt uneasy.

s0030.literal: At that time Han Zigao was in the capital; his men and horses had always been numerous. Yu each time rode in a small carriage, cloaked in women's dress, to plot with Zigao.
s0030.idiomatic: Han Zigao was then in the capital with a large following of men and horses. Yu would ride in a small carriage dressed as a woman to plot with him.

s0031.literal: Zigao's army commander reported the affair. Emperor Xuan arrested Zigao, Zhongju, and Yu and handed them over to the Court of Trials.
s0031.idiomatic: One of Zigao’s army commanders reported the affair. Emperor Xuan seized Zigao, Zhongju, and Yu and sent them to the court of trials.

s0032.literal: An edict said: "Dao Zhongju is a mediocre, petty talent who by chance enjoyed high rank; he received office from the former court and glory and favor were lofty and bright—father participating in royal government, son holding a great commandery, ritual grand in affinal kinship, power equal to the imperial clan.
s0032.idiomatic: An edict declared: “Dao Zhongju is a mediocre man raised by luck. The former court heaped rank on him: father in the government, son in a great commandery, affinal honors as grand as kinship, power to match the imperial clan.

s0033.literal: Yet he indulged this arrogant darkness, insulted and defied the hundred offices; at the beginning of the mourning silence he usurped state government, expelled worthy kin, and scorned the Terrace posts.
s0033.idiomatic: Yet he grew arrogant and dark, insulting every office. At the start of the mourning silence he seized the government, drove out worthy kin, and mocked the Terrace.

s0034.literal: Han Zigao is a trifling, minute man, promoted from the lowest ranks, entered to join the palace guard, entrusted with the innermost confidence—yet the bee and scorpion have poison, and he dared turn to bite.
s0034.idiomatic: Han Zigao is a nothing raised from the gutter. He entered the palace guard and won the innermost trust, yet like a bee or scorpion he turned to bite.

s0035.literal: Zhongju and Zigao, together outer and inner, secretly wove treacherous plots and in secret made separate plans.
s0035.idiomatic: Zhongju and Zigao worked as outer shell and inner core, weaving treason in secret.

s0036.literal: The Prince of Ancheng is Our uncle; in kinship none is heavier. He received the charge to guide and uplift, inherited the entrusted care; because We are young and weak, he ought to protect and preserve Us.
s0036.idiomatic: The Prince of Ancheng is my uncle, the closest of kin. He was charged to guide the state and bear the late emperor’s trust. Because I am young, he should protect me.

s0037.literal: The safety of house and state rests with the chief ministers; the weight of Yi and Zhou—no one disputes it; the old ministers among generals and chancellors all know to look up to him as the standard.
s0037.idiomatic: The realm’s safety belongs to its chief ministers. The weight of Yi and Zhou is beyond dispute. Every old general and minister knows to look to him.

s0038.literal: Yet they gathered wicked followers, intending a surprise attack; they massed at the Eastern City and pressed upon Chongli, planning to set up Zhongju to seize state power, to drive off the Minister of Works with intent to monopolize government, secretly joining factions and parties, and were about to endanger the altars of state.
s0038.idiomatic: Yet they gathered villains for a surprise strike, massed at the Eastern City and pressed Chongli, meant to set up Zhongju and seize power, drive off the minister of works and rule alone, knit secret factions, and were about to endanger the dynasty.

s0039.literal: Relying on the spirits of the ancestors, the treacherous plot was exposed.
s0039.idiomatic: Thanks to the ancestors’ spirits, the plot came to light.

s0040.literal: The former magistrate of Shangyu, Lu Fang, and others fully reported the affair, and there is corroborating evidence; they fixed the seventh day of this month to carry out their wicked plot.
s0040.idiomatic: The former magistrate of Shangyu, Lu Fang, and others laid out the whole affair with proof. They had set the seventh of this month for the crime.

s0041.literal: Area Commander Mingche, Left Guard General and Commandant of the Guards Bao'an, and the various dukes and others also all knew of the affair.
s0041.idiomatic: Area commander Mingche, left guard general and commandant of the guards Bao’an, and the other dukes knew it as well.

s0042.literal: Two or three traces are plain in court and countryside; their contrary way and betrayed virtue horrify all who hear and see.
s0042.idiomatic: Their tracks show in court and country alike. Their treason shocks every eye and ear.

s0043.literal: Now the great villain is destroyed and the guilty are caught; all may be taken and handed to the Court of Trials to rectify the penal code.
s0043.idiomatic: Now the great villain is cut down and the guilty taken. Let all be sent to the court of trials and judged by law.

s0044.literal: Guilt stops with Zhongju, father and son, and Zigao—three persons only; the rest are wholly pardoned and will not be questioned.
s0044.idiomatic: Guilt ends with Zhongju, his son, and Zigao—three people only. All others are wholly pardoned and will not be questioned.

s0045.literal: " Zhongju and Yu were both granted death in prison; he was fifty-one years old.
s0045.idiomatic: ” Zhongju and Yu were granted death in prison. He was fifty-one.

s0046.literal: Yu's sons and daughters, as the emperor's affinal kin, were pardoned.
s0046.idiomatic: Yu’s sons and daughters were spared as the emperor’s affinal kin.

s0047.literal: Han Zigao was a native of Shanyin in Kuaiji.
s0047.idiomatic: Han Zigao came from Shanyin in Kuaiji.

s0048.literal: His family was originally of very low status.

s0049.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion he sojourned in the capital.
s0049.idiomatic: During Hou Jing’s rebellion he stayed in the capital.

s0050.literal: When Jing was pacified Emperor Wen went out to hold Wu Commandery. Zigao was sixteen, in the age of the hair knot; his appearance was beautiful and his bearing like a woman's. At Huai Ford he attached to a convoy wishing to return home. Emperor Wen saw him and asked, "Can you serve me?
s0050.idiomatic: After Jing fell, Emperor Wen went out to hold Wu Commandery. Zigao was sixteen, still wearing the boy’s knot, beautiful as a woman. At Huai Ford he joined a convoy bound home. Emperor Wen saw him and asked, “Will you serve me?

s0052.literal: Zigao's original name was Manzi; Emperor Wen changed his name.
s0052.idiomatic: His name had been Manzi; Emperor Wen renamed him.

s0053.literal: By nature he was respectful and careful, diligent in service, always holding the belt knife for personal attendance and passing wine and roasted meat.
s0053.idiomatic: He was respectful and careful, always at hand with the belt knife, pouring wine and serving roast meat.

s0054.literal: Emperor Wen was quick-tempered by nature; Zigao always grasped his intent.
s0054.idiomatic: Emperor Wen was quick-tempered; Zigao always read his mind.

s0055.literal: When he grew older he gradually learned horsemanship and archery; he had considerable daring and resolution and wished to be a commander; when Du Kan was pacified he was given troops.
s0055.idiomatic: As he grew he learned riding and archery, showed daring, and wanted to be a commander. When Du Kan fell, he was given troops.

s0056.literal: Emperor Wen cherished him exceedingly and never let him leave his side.
s0056.idiomatic: Emperor Wen doted on him and never let him leave his side.

s0057.literal: Emperor Wen once dreamed he rode a horse up a mountain; the road was perilous and he was about to fall; Zigao pushed and supported him so he ascended.
s0057.idiomatic: Emperor Wen once dreamed he rode uphill on a perilous path about to fall. Zigao pushed and lifted him up.

s0058.literal: When the Founder campaigned against Zhang Biao, Shen Tai and others had already surrendered; the Founder held the prefectural city, and Zhou Wenyü garrisoned north of the city at Xiang
s0058.idiomatic: When the Founder campaigned against Zhang Biao, Shen Tai and others had already surrendered. The Founder held the prefectural city, and Zhou Wenyü garrisoned north of the city at Xiang

s0061.literal: Editorial footnote marker 1. Zhang Biao returned by night from Shan county to raid the city. The Founder went out through the northern gate. In the sudden rush of dark evening the soldiers were in turmoil; Wenyü too had not yet determined where the Founder was—only Zigao was at his side. The Founder then sent Zigao from amid the disorderly troops to go see Wenyü, return with orders and replies, and in the dark go again to comfort the armies.
s0061.idiomatic: [1] Zhang Biao returned by night from Shan county to storm the city. The Founder slipped out the north gate. In the sudden dark the troops panicked. Wenyü did not know where the Founder was—only Zigao stood beside him. The Founder sent Zigao through the chaos to Wenyü, bring back his orders, then go again in the dark to steady the army.

s0062.literal: The Founder's scattered troops gradually gathered; Zigao led him into Wenyü's camp, and together they built palisades.
s0062.idiomatic: The Founder’s scattered men slowly gathered. Zigao led him into Wenyü’s camp and together they threw up palisades.

s0063.literal: The next day they fought Biao; Biao's general Shen Jin surrendered again Editorial footnote marker 2. Biao fled to Song mountain; eastern Zhe was pacified.
s0063.idiomatic: The next day they fought Biao. Biao’s general Shen Jin surrendered again. [2] Biao fled to Song mountain and eastern Zhe was pacified.

s0064.literal: The Founder then assigned many of his subordinates to Zigao; Zigao also was generous with wealth and courteous to officers; those who came to him were very numerous.
s0064.idiomatic: The Founder then gave Zigao many of his own followers. Zigao was generous and courteous to officers, and men flocked to him.

s0065.literal: When Emperor Xuan entered to assist in government, Zigao's military authority was excessive; he felt deeply ill at ease, liked to visit the Terrace offices, and also sought to go out to the garrisons of Heng and Guang.
s0065.idiomatic: When Emperor Xuan entered to govern, Zigao’s military power weighed too heavy. Uneasy, he frequented the Terrace offices and asked to be posted to Heng and Guang.

s0066.literal: Eighth month, first year of Guangda: the former magistrate of Shangyu, Lu Fang, and Zigao's army commander reported his plotting rebellion. Emperor Xuan was in the Masters of Writing office and thereupon summoned civil and military officials in post to discuss establishing the crown prince. Zigao was among them; at dawn he entered the office, was seized, and sent to the Court of Trials. That evening he was granted death together with Dao Zhongju; he was thirty years old.
s0066.idiomatic: In the eighth month of Guangda year 1 (567), the former magistrate of Shangyu, Lu Fang, and one of Zigao’s army commanders reported a plot to rebel. Emperor Xuan was in the masters of writing office and called the officials to discuss the crown prince. Zigao came at dawn, was seized and sent to the court of trials, and that evening was granted death with Dao Zhongju. He was thirty.

s0067.literal: His father Yanqing and sons and younger brothers were all pardoned.
s0067.idiomatic: His father Yanqing and his brothers and sons were all pardoned.

s0068.literal: Yanqing, because of Zigao's favor, reached Attendant of the Secretariat and Magistrate of Shanyin.
s0068.idiomatic: Through Zigao’s favor Yanqing rose to secretariat attendant and magistrate of Shanyin.

s0069.literal: Wang Lin marched east; Jiao followed Hou Tian to resist him.
s0069.idiomatic: When Wang Lin marched east, Jiao followed Hou Tian to resist him.

s0070.literal: When Lin was pacified, [Jiao] garrisoned Pen city and oversaw Jiangzhou affairs.
s0070.idiomatic: When Lin fell, Jiao garrisoned Pen city and ran Jiangzhou affairs.

s0071.literal: At that time the prefects and magistrates of the southern provinces were mostly local chieftains and strongmen who did not obey court law; Emperor Wen ordered Jiao to rein them in by law.
s0071.idiomatic: Southern prefects and magistrates were often local strongmen who ignored the court. Emperor Wen ordered Jiao to bring them to heel by law.

s0072.literal: When Wang Lin was routed and scattered, generals and soldiers mostly attached themselves to Jiao.
s0072.idiomatic: When Wang Lin’s army broke up, his officers and men mostly joined Jiao.

s0073.literal: In the third year he was appointed provisional credentials, Regular Attendant Direct Communication, Benevolent and Martial General, and salary as Inspector of Xinzhou, supervising Jiangzhou.
s0073.idiomatic: In the third year he was given provisional credentials, direct-communication regular attendant, benevolent and martial general, and inspector of Xinzhou’s salary while supervising Jiangzhou.

s0074.literal: Soon an edict ordered him to supervise military affairs in the five commanderies of Xunyang, Taiyuan, Gaotang, South and North Xincai, and made him Administrator of Xunyang; provisional credentials, general, provincial salary, and supervision remained as before.
s0074.idiomatic: Soon he was ordered to command armies in Xunyang, Taiyuan, Gaotang, and North and South Xincai and was made administrator of Xunyang, keeping his credentials, general’s title, salary, and supervision.

s0075.literal: Zhou Di plotted rebellion and sent his elder brother's son to lie in ambush aboard ship, falsely claiming to be merchants, intending to strike Jiao at Pen city.
s0075.idiomatic: Zhou Di rebelled and sent his nephew with hidden troops aboard ship, posing as merchants, to strike Jiao at Pen city.

s0076.literal: Before it was launched the affair was discovered; Jiao sent men to intercept them and seized all their ships and arms.
s0076.idiomatic: Before they moved, the plot was found out. Jiao sent men against them and took all their ships and weapons.

s0077.literal: That year Jiao followed Area Commander Wu Mingche to campaign against Di; when Di was pacified, by merit he was appointed Regular Attendant, General Who Pacifies the South, and Administrator of Linchuan, advanced in rank to marquis, his fief increased together with the previous to five hundred households.
s0077.idiomatic: That year Jiao followed area commander Wu Mingche against Di. When Di fell, he was made regular attendant, general who pacifies the south, and administrator of Linchuan, raised to marquis with five hundred households in all.

s0078.literal: Before he took up the appointment he entered court and was thereupon given credentials, made Area Commander over military affairs in the four provinces of Xiang, Ba, and others, and Inspector of Xiangzhou; regular attendant and general remained as before.
s0078.idiomatic: Before he took office he went to court and was given credentials as area commander over Xiang, Ba, and the other provinces and made inspector of Xiangzhou, retaining his attendant and general titles.

s0079.literal: Jiao rose from a low clerk, was skilled at managing property; the lands of the Xiang river region produce much, and what he obtained all entered the court—grain transport, bamboo and timber, the deliveries entrusted were very numerous;
s0079.idiomatic: Jiao rose from a petty clerk and knew how to build wealth. The Xiang region yields much, and he sent it all to court—grain, bamboo, timber, and convoys beyond count;

s0080.literal: as for oil, honey, dried meats, vegetables, and the like, there was nothing he did not supply.
s0080.idiomatic: As for oil, honey, cured meats, and vegetables—nothing was left unprovided.

s0081.literal: He also campaigned in the river valleys and cave settlements and brought in many bronze drums and captives, all sent to the capital.
s0081.idiomatic: He also fought the hill peoples and sent bronze drums and captives to the capital in great numbers.

s0082.literal: When the Deposed Emperor came to the throne, [Jiao's] title was advanced to General Who Pacifies the South, his enfeoffment changed to Marquis of Chong'an county, Editorial footnote marker 4. fief one thousand five hundred households.
s0082.idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor succeeded, Jiao was made general who pacifies the south and re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Chong’an [4] with one thousand five hundred households.

s0083.literal: Emperor Wen, because Xiangzhou produced fir timber for boats, ordered Jiao to build more than two hundred great ships of the Golden-Wing type and all equipment for river warfare, intending to enter the Han and the Gorges.
s0083.idiomatic: Emperor Wen, since Xiangzhou furnished fir for ships, ordered Jiao to build more than two hundred Golden-Wing great ships and all river-war gear, intending to enter the Han and the gorges.

s0084.literal: After Han Zigao was executed, Jiao felt ill at ease within and repaired armor and gathered followers, treating the prefects and magistrates under him with lavish courtesy.
s0084.idiomatic: After Zigao’s death Jiao grew uneasy, armored men and gathered followers, and lavished gifts on his subordinate officials.

s0085.literal: Emperor Xuan repeatedly ordered Jiao to send the great Golden-Wing ships and the like; he put off and delayed and did not arrive.
s0085.idiomatic: Emperor Xuan repeatedly ordered him to send the Golden-Wing great ships. Jiao stalled and would not deliver.

s0086.literal: In the first year of Guangda he secretly memorialized asking for Guangzhou to observe the court's intent; Emperor Xuan falsely assented, but the edict had not yet been issued.
s0086.idiomatic: In Guangda year 1 (567) he secretly asked for Guangzhou to test the court’s mind. Emperor Xuan pretended to agree, but no edict had yet gone out.

s0087.literal: Jiao also sent envoys to draw in Northern Zhou troops and further honored Xiao Kui as sovereign; his warriors and horses were very numerous.
s0087.idiomatic: Jiao also sent envoys to draw in Northern Zhou troops and set up Xiao Kui as his sovereign. His army grew very large.

s0088.literal: An edict then made Wu Mingche Inspector of Xiangzhou, in fact intending to strike him with light troops.
s0088.idiomatic: An edict then named Wu Mingche inspector of Xiangzhou, intending in truth to strike Jiao with a light force.

s0089.literal: At that time, fearing Jiao would strike first, they first sent Mingche at the head of thirty thousand men, riding Golden-Wing [ships] straight for Yingzhou, and also sent Pacifying-the-Army Grand General Chunyu Liang at the head of fifty thousand men, riding great ships to follow after, and also ordered Provisional Credentials, Crowned-with-Martiality General Yang Wentong to set out separately from An
s0089.idiomatic: Fearing Jiao would move first, they sent Mingche with thirty thousand men in Golden-Wing ships straight for Yingzhou, and pacifying-the-army grand general Chunyu Liang with fifty thousand in great ships behind him, and ordered provisional-credentials crowned-with-martiality general Yang Wentong by a separate route from An

s0091.literal: [Cheng] by the foot-path out through Chaling, Editorial footnote marker 5. and also ordered Administrator of Bashan Huang Fahui to set out separately from Yiyang through Liling to make a surprise attack, taking him unawares, and together with Inspector of Jiangzhou Zhang Zhaoda, Inspector of Yingzhou Cheng Lingxi, and others to consult on suppressing the rebel.
s0091.idiomatic: [Cheng] by the foot-path through Chaling, [5] and ordered Bashan administrator Huang Fahui from Yiyang through Liling for a surprise blow, together with Jiangzhou inspector Zhang Zhaoda, Yingzhou inspector Cheng Lingxi, and others to plan the suppression.

s0092.literal: At that time Xiao Kui sent a river fleet to support Jiao.
s0092.idiomatic: Xiao Kui then sent a river fleet to support Jiao.

s0093.literal: Emperor Wu of Zhou also sent his younger brother the Duke of Weiguo, Yuwen Zhi, at the head of troops garrisoned at Lushan, and also sent his Pillar of State the Duke of Chang, Tuoba Ding, with thirty thousand men and horses to attack and besiege Yingzhou.
s0093.idiomatic: Emperor Wu of Zhou also sent his brother the Duke of Weiguo, Yuwen Zhi, to camp at Lushan, and his pillar of state Tuoba Ding with thirty thousand troops to besiege Yingzhou.

s0094.literal: Xiao Kui appointed Jiao Minister of Works; Dai Sengshuo, Administrator of Ba; Ren Mannu, Interior Minister of Hengyang; Pan Zhizhen, Interior Minister of Baling; Zhang Zhaoyu, Administrator of Yueyang;
s0094.idiomatic: Xiao Kui made Jiao minister of works and set Dai Sengshuo over Ba, Ren Mannu over Hengyang, Pan Zhizhen over Baling, and Zhang Zhaoyu over Yueyang;

s0096.literal: [Gui]yang Administrator Cao Xuan, Editorial footnote marker 6. Administrator of Xiangdong Qian Ming, and all were placed under Jiao.
s0096.idiomatic: [Gui]yang administrator Cao Xuan, [6] Xiangdong administrator Qian Ming, and others—all under Jiao’s command.

s0097.literal: Also Administrator of Changsha Cao Qing and others had originally been under Jiao and therefore served his use.
s0097.idiomatic: Changsha administrator Cao Qing and others had already been Jiao’s men and now served him.

s0098.literal: The Emperor feared that the officials commanding the upper Yangtze would all be swayed by Jiao, and thereupon issued an edict saying: "The rebel Jiao is of cart-and-servant mean birth; he happened to meet with reward and promotion, was entrusted with a frontier post and ought to have received favored care, yet he turned against what nurtured him and raised treacherous plots, set up the Xiao house, their covenant and pact plain to see, poison and malice in his heart, his aim to endanger the altars of state, inciting the border regions, driving and pressing scholars and commoners, ants massed in Ba and Xiang, pigs charging at Yan and Ying, opposing Heaven and turning against earth—men and spirits alike rage.
s0098.idiomatic: The emperor feared upstream governors would side with Jiao and issued an edict: “The traitor Jiao rose from cart and stable. Promoted by chance to a frontier post, he should have been grateful. Instead he rebelled, enthroned the Xiao line, sealed open pacts, and aimed at the dynasty. He stirred the borders, drove the people, swarmed Ba and Xiang like ants, and charged Yan and Ying like boars—heaven and earth alike revile him.

s0099.literal: Campaigning-South General Liang, Pacifying-South General Mingche, and Inspector of Yingzhou Lingxi received the law and led the dedicated campaign, exhausting mind and strength, comforting and encouraging the fierce and heroic; the river forces advanced together; righteous valor vied in ardor; the vicious and wicked ran to destruction; reports of victory came one after another; heavy miasma was cleared away again and again. Speaking of weeping over guilt, We think of renewal.
s0099.idiomatic: Campaigning-south general Liang, pacifying-south general Mingche, and Yingzhou inspector Lingxi took the law and marched with all their strength, heartening the brave as the fleets advanced together. Valor flared, the wicked were crushed, victory reports came in waves, and the foul air cleared. In judging guilt I look to renewal.

s0100.literal: A partial pardon may be granted to the two provinces of Xiang and Ba: all who were compelled by the rebels and took part in the wicked faction are wholly not to be questioned;
s0100.idiomatic: Let Xiang and Ba be partly pardoned: all who were forced into the rebel ranks and joined the guilty faction shall go unquestioned;
